title: Binary Tree Upside Down
statement:
You get the `root` of a binary tree (possibly empty) with a special shape: every right child has a left sibling (its parent also has a left child), and every right child is a leaf. Turn the tree upside down and return the new root.

The flip follows the path of left children from the root. For every parent `P` with left child `L` and right child `R` (`R` may be missing):

- `L` takes `R` as its new left child and `P` as its new right child.
- The original root keeps no children, so it becomes a leaf.

The last node on that left path (the one with no left child) becomes the new root. An empty tree stays empty.
constraints: The tree has between 0 and 10 nodes
Every right node has a sibling (a left node with the same parent)
Every right node has no children
notes:
## Intuition

Look only at the path of left children: `root`, `root.left`, `root.left.left`, ... Flipping the tree reverses that path, much like reversing a linked list, and each right child simply rides along as the new left child of its sibling. Recursion handles the reversal naturally: first flip everything below `root.left`, then hang `root` and its right child under `root.left` on the way back up. An iterative version that collects the left path in an array works too.

## Approach

1. If `root` is empty or has no left child, it is already the bottom of the left path; return it as the new root.
2. Recursively flip the subtree of `root.left`; its result `newRoot` is the root of the whole answer.
3. `root.left` is now the lowest node of the flipped part. Give it `root.right` as its left child and `root` as its right child.
4. Clear `root.left` and `root.right`, since `root` now sits at the bottom.
5. Return `newRoot` all the way up.

## Example 1, step by step

`root = [1,2,3,4,5]`. The recursion goes down the left path 1 → 2 → 4. Node `4` has no left child, so it is `newRoot`. Back at `2`: node `4` gets left `5` and right `2`, and `2` loses its children. Back at `1`: node `2` gets left `3` and right `1`, and `1` loses its children. The answer is `[4,5,2,null,null,3,1]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(h), where h is the length of the left path; each node on it is rewired once.
- Space: O(h) for the recursion stack.

## Pitfalls

- Clear `root.left` and `root.right` at the end; otherwise the old root still points to its children and the tree contains a cycle.
- Rewire through `root.left` before clearing it; once `root.left` is `null` you have lost the node to attach to.
- Return `newRoot` from every level, not `root`: the answer's root is the bottom of the left path.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` | the node being flipped at this level of recursion |
| `newRoot` | the bottom of the left path, root of the flipped tree |
| `root.left` | the former left child, which becomes `root`'s parent |
| `root.right` | the former right child, which becomes the left child of `root.left` |

narration.2: An empty tree, or a node with no left child, is the bottom of the left path.
narration.3: That node is already the root of its flipped subtree.
narration.5: Flip everything under the left child first; its result is the final root.
narration.6: The old right child becomes the left child of the old left child.
narration.7: The current node itself becomes the right child of its old left child.
narration.8: Drop the old left link so the tree has no cycle.
narration.9: Drop the old right link too; this node is now a leaf.
narration.10: Pass the new root back up unchanged.
